054 - The Onion and Philosophy - Fake Ne: The Onion is the satirical newspaper famous for deadpan fake headlines like 'World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent' and 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer', read here alongside its syndicated advice columns. Its satire is philosophical on purpose: the essays treat ridicule as a tool for exposing self-deception, ask whether belief in God survives the evidence, probe the morality of swearing and of calling someone an asshole, and wonder whether every generation thinks the next one is dumber. Voltaire would recognize the project.
055 - Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger: Doctor Who is the BBC's long-running science fiction series (since 1963) about the Doctor, a time-traveling alien who explores the universe in the TARDIS and, when mortally wounded, regenerates into a new body and personality. That regeneration gimmick alone raises hard questions about what makes someone the same person, and the show piles on more: time-travel paradoxes, whether the Daleks could count as people, what makes the Doctor's mercy special, and what his wonder-struck companions teach us about the love of wisdom.
056 - Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way: Dune is Frank Herbert's 1965 science fiction epic, set on the desert planet Arrakis, where the young noble Paul Atreides gains messianic power over the Fremen and the spice that drives interstellar civilization. The essays wrestle with what Herbert built into the story: whether Paul's foreseen future leaves any room for freedom, the ethics of the Bene Gesserit's breeding programs and Leto II's tyrannical Golden Path, the test of what makes a human, war and empire, and a religion and ecology that read uncomfortably like our own politics.
057 - Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mi: Rush is the Canadian power trio of Geddy Lee, Alex Lifeson and Neil Peart, beloved since the 1970s for virtuosic, intricately structured rock with lyrics about science, individualism and dystopias, and just as famously polarizing among critics. The essays ask whether the band deserves its reputation as a 'thinking man's band': is complex rhythm really mind opposed to body, does Neil Peart owe anything to Ayn Rand, what makes a cover or a drum-along faithful, and what Rush's cult of craft says about taste, technique and authenticity.
058 - Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over: Dexter is the Showtime drama (2006-2013) about Dexter Morgan, a Miami forensic technician who is also a serial killer, channeling his urges into murdering murderers under the strict rules his foster father called Harry's Code. That premise makes him a perfect laboratory for ethics: can a remorseless sociopath be decent or even praiseworthy, is he blameworthy for urges born of childhood trauma, does his 'be sure' rule ever amount to knowledge of guilt, and what do his emotionless life and vigilante justice reveal about what a good life requires?
059 - Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Ev: Halo is the blockbuster Xbox science fiction game series launched in 2001, casting the player as Master Chief, a faceless super-soldier fighting the alien Covenant alongside the AI Cortana. The essays argue there is more going on than shooting aliens: which of a million players' Master Chiefs is the real one, whether Cortana could pass the Turing test, whether the Spartan program's child-soldiers live absurd or Stoic lives, whether Plato would count Halo as guardian training, and what a game owes us if it wants to count as art.
060 - SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosop: SpongeBob SquarePants is the Nickelodeon cartoon (since 1999) about an irrepressibly cheerful sea sponge who flips Krabby Patties in the underwater town of Bikini Bottom, adored by children and adults alike. The essays find real philosophy under the sea: SpongeBob as Aristotle's virtuous mean, the happy ignoramus Patrick measured against Mill's discontented Socrates, Squidward as Schopenhauer's suffering will, Mr. Krabs's money worship weighed against Marx and Adam Smith, Sandy Cheeks as feminist scientist, and what it takes to have the best day ever.
061 - Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - T: Sherlock Holmes is Arthur Conan Doyle's legendary consulting detective (from 1887), who solves apparently impossible cases from Baker Street by minute observation and startling inference, alongside his chronicler Dr. Watson. The essays treat the canon, and its screen Holmeses, as a philosophical quarry: are Holmes's deductions knowledge or luck, how does abduction actually work, is he Spinoza's free man or Nietzsche's self-fashioned overman, what makes his friendship with Watson the best kind, and does his method anticipate Heidegger?
062 - Inception and Philosophy - Ideas t: Inception is Christopher Nolan's 2010 film about thieves who enter people's dreams to steal, and plant, ideas, ending on the spinning top that may or may not tell Cobb he is awake. The essays use it to dig into skepticism and the self: how do we know we are not dreaming, what is wrong with planting a thought in someone's mind, can our very thoughts be other than our own, does Nozick's experience machine explain why Cobb leaves Limbo, and is the happy ending a choice rather than a proof.
063 - Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do: Philip K. Dick is the science fiction author whose paranoid novels and stories inspired Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report and The Adjustment Bureau, works where false memories, androids indistinguishable from people, and manipulated realities are the norm. The essays trace what Hollywood keeps losing in adaptation: Dick's dark vision of accepted unfreedom and permanent doubt against the silver screen's free will and happy endings, whether Deckard could be an android without any evidence settling it, and whether the ancient skeptics' tranquility is the only sane response.
